newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court to decide school religion case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court to decide school religion case.

text.p: The Supreme Court agreed Friday to hear a Clinton administration appeal seeking to overturn a 12-year-old ruling that barred public school teachers from conducting remedial classes at parochial schools.

The high court said it will consider the administration's arguments that the 1985 ruling had an adverse impact on providing educational and counselling services to low-income students who need remedial aid in public and private schools.
The Clinton administration, New York City and parents of a group of parochial schoolchildren asked the justices to reopen the long-running legal dispute.

The high court by a 5-4 vote ruled in 1985 that publicly paid teachers may not offer remedial classes on parochial school grounds. Such programmes violate the constitutional requirement on church-state separation, it said.

But the court has become more conservative over the past 12 years, lowering the wall of separation between church and state. The justices will hear arguments in the case in April, and a decision will be due by the end of June.

The Supreme Court's 1985 decision did not ban public school teachers from helping parochial students. Such help is allowed under a 1965 federal law. But the ruling barred public school teachers paid with federal funds from teaching remedial classes for disadvantaged children in religiously affiliated schools.

Acting Solicitor General Walter Dellinger, the administration's top courtroom lawyer, told the high court hundreds of millions of dollars have been spent by public schoool systems nationwide to comply with the 1985 decision.

He said much of the money has gone to transport parochial school students to public schools for special classes. Other alternatives have been renting mobile classrooms and computer-assisted instruction.

A federal judge and a U.S. appeals court refused to reopen the case, rejecting pleas from the New York City Board of Education citing newly discovered evidence about the financial burden from the ruling.

Dellinger, whose arguments were filed on behalf of Education Secretary Richard Riley, said "intervening circumstances" and the court's more recent church-state rulings warrant reconsideration of the ruling.
The Supreme Court "does have the authority to overrule its own prior decisions, even in the same case," he said.
The Education Department under the Reagan administration took the same position that public school teachers should be allowed to conduct the classes at religious schools.
Stanley Geller, an attorney for the six individuals who won the 1985 ruling, urged the Supreme Court to reject the appeal.
Alternatively, if the high court wants to reconsider the ruling, then it should send the case back to the federal judge for a hearing and possible trial, he said.
